response.reasoning:
Both of you agree on most of what happened: four retired sets were sold for £200, the buyer asked before buying whether the boxes were in good condition and was told they had been stored in a cupboard since new and were fine, and the listing itself promised boxes in good condition. So box condition was plainly part of what was being paid for, and it is measured against that promise. The parcel was delivered and the buyer said something was wrong the same day, which is prompt and consistent with damage found on opening rather than something that developed later.

What the photographs show is a single shipping carton with one corner crushed and split, and one set box with a crumpled, dented corner in the same place. The rest of that box is intact, and there is nothing to suggest the other three sets are affected. Taken together, the two pictures read as a transit impact to one corner of the parcel that carried through to one of the four boxes. I accept the seller's account that the sets left in good order; I also accept the buyer's account that one box did not arrive that way. Those two things are not in conflict.

That leaves the loss to be allocated rather than blame to be assigned. The seller chose the packaging and is the one who undertook to deliver boxes in good condition; a single carton with the sets against its corner is what let one impact reach a box. But the buyer has received four sets, all the contents, and three boxes matching the description, and the fourth box is dented and split at one corner rather than destroyed — the set is still usable and still saleable, at a reduced price for a collector who cares about the box.

My estimate of the shortfall is roughly a quarter of what was paid: the affected set is about a quarter of the order, its box damage takes a substantial bite out of that set's value given how much of the price rides on box condition, and a modest allowance on top reflects that the packing choice was the seller's. Twenty-five per cent of the money held to the buyer, seventy-five per cent to the seller, leaves the buyer paying roughly what four sets are worth with one dented box, and leaves the seller with the price of what actually arrived intact.

findings.statement: Before buying, the buyer asked specifically whether the boxes were in good condition and said that for retired sets the box is most of what is being paid for; the seller answered that they had been stored in a cupboard since new and the boxes were fine.
The listing described four retired sets, used and like new, with boxes in good condition, at £200, so box condition is part of what was promised.
The parcel was handed to the carrier on 26 August, moved through depots, and was delivered on 28 August; the buyer reported the damage the same day it arrived.
The photograph of the outer shipping carton shows one top corner crushed and split open, marked fragile, with no sign of a second protective outer layer.

The photograph of the set inside shows a single set box with a crumpled and dented corner at the top left, in the same position as the crushed corner of the shipping carton, while the rest of the box front and its printing are intact.
Only one box is shown as damaged; nothing in the material suggests the other three sets or their boxes were affected, and no missing or broken contents are alleged.
The seller states the sets were in good condition when they left and were packed carefully; this is consistent with the damage pattern being a single transit impact rather than a pre-existing fault.
